questions.q: In this course, what does “Anti-TERT” refer to?
options: The enzyme that seals the final gap in a newly synthesised DNA strand.
An antisense oligonucleotide that degrades TERT mRNA, so the cell can no longer rebuild chromosome ends.
questions.why: Anti-TERT is an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO): it does not attack the enzyme directly, it degrades TERT's messenger RNA. TERT encodes the catalytic subunit of telomerase, so the cell can no longer make telomerase and can no longer rebuild chromosome ends. The lecturer's preclinical data from lecture four is this: in subcutaneous xenografts in immunodeficient nude mice, the untreated group had a tumour take rate of 9/12, while after 3 weeks of anti-TERT pretreatment only 2/12 remained (Fisher p = 0.01). The other three options describe the enzyme that seals the gap, the wild-type baseline and hepatocytes.

questions.q: Of the three models of DNA replication compared in the Meselson–Stahl isotope-labelling experiment, what is the model in which “the old strands are broken up and mixed into the new strands” called?
questions.why: The three models of DNA replication are conservative (the old duplex stays intact and a new one is built alongside), semi-conservative (each new duplex carries one old strand) and dispersive (the old strands are cut into fragments and dispersed into the new strands). The experimental results support semi-conservative, so dispersive is ruled out; isotope labelling is needed to tell the three apart because the results alone do not show which old strand has gone where, so the label has to be tracked. The other three options are the name of semi-conservative replication, of the replication bubble opened at each origin, and of a single-strand break, none of which is the name of a replication model.

questions.q: What is the function of DNA ligase?
options: The enzyme that unwinds the two DNA strands so that they can be replicated.
The exonuclease that removes the RNA primer from the DNA.
The enzyme that builds a new DNA chain, adding nucleotides only in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
The enzyme that seals the final gap in a newly synthesised DNA strand.
questions.why: DNA ligase seals nicks, joining a 5′ phosphate to a 3′ hydroxyl with a phosphodiester bond. Once the Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand have each been synthesised, an RNA primer and a seam are still left between them; after RNase H removes the RNA primer, the remaining gap is closed by ligase, and only then do the fragments become one continuous strand. The same principle is used in recombinant DNA and molecular cloning, where sticky ends produced by restriction enzymes are joined in the same way. The other three options describe the unwinding enzyme, the exonuclease that removes RNA primers and the enzyme that synthesises the new strand.

questions.q: What is the English name for the enzyme that builds a new DNA chain and adds nucleotides only in the 5′ to 3′ direction?
questions.why: DNA polymerase has only one hand, so it can only reach in one direction: it adds new nucleotides to the 3′ end of the strand being extended, which is why DNA can only be synthesised from the 5′ end towards the 3′ end. The same enzyme also carries 3′→5′ exonuclease proofreading activity: when it catches a mismatch (for example A:G), it cuts out the wrong base and puts the correct one in its place. A proofreading-defective polymerase generates lots of mutations and neoantigens, so the tumour responds well to immune checkpoint inhibitors. The other three options are the exonuclease responsible for proofreading, the enzyme that lays down the RNA primer and the enzyme that relieves torsional strain.

questions.q: “_____” means deoxyribonucleotide triphosphate, a nucleotide carrying three phosphate groups that serves as the free-nucleotide raw material for DNA synthesis.
questions.why: The polymerase removes one phosphate from the 5′ end of each dNTP and adds the remaining two to the 3′-OH of the new strand, releasing pyrophosphate; PCR can amplify precisely because every cycle turns these raw materials into new duplexes. The concentration of the raw material is also one of the reaction conditions: too little makes the reaction too slow, too much easily produces non-specific products. The other three options describe the antisense oligonucleotide that degrades TERT mRNA, the RNA template component of telomerase and the transmission electron microscope.

questions.q: In this course, what does a tumour's Drug resistance refer to?
options: The tumour no longer responds to a drug it was previously sensitive to. It can be caused by a new mutation, or by an isoform that has lost the drug-binding site.
The state in which cells stop dividing without dying.
The number of times human cells can divide before they are forced to stop.
DNA polymerase cannot replicate the very end of a linear chromosome, so the telomere shortens at every division.
questions.why: Drug resistance has three sources. At the gene level, a new mutation changes the drug-binding site, or lets downstream signalling bypass the blocked point. At the splicing level, alternative splicing produces a different isoform that splices out the exon carrying the drug-binding site, so the same gene and the same drug no longer have a binding site (the AR-V7 on the slides is the product of a cryptic exon in AR, an activated form that confers enzalutamide resistance). At the replication level, the 3′→5′ proofreading activity of the polymerase excises nucleoside analogue drugs from the DNA. The other three options describe cellular senescence, the upper limit on the number of cell divisions and the end-replication problem, none of which is a change in drug response.

questions.q: In DNA replication, what does the End-replication problem refer to?
options: The marked position on the DNA where replication begins.
The counting mechanism that turns cell division into a limit on “how many times one cell can divide”.
The protein that shortens over-long telomeres by cutting away the t-loop.
DNA polymerase cannot replicate the very end of a linear chromosome, so the telomere shortens at every division.
questions.why: DNA can only be synthesised 5′→3′, and once the RNA primer at the end of the lagging strand has been removed there is no 3′ end for anything to be added to, so a gap is left at the chromosome end that can never be filled. Each somatic division shortens the telomere by about 50 to 200 base pairs; once it reaches a threshold the cell enters senescence, and that is the Hayflick limit. Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase with an internal RNA template and can extend the 3′ overhang back; it is active in embryonic stem cells and germ cells, and in cancer it is commonly reactivated (about 90% of cancers upregulate telomerase). The other three options describe the origin of replication, the counting mechanism for the number of divisions and the protein that trims over-long telomeres.

questions.q: When the lecturer draws DNA polymerase as a machine with two domains, what does the EXO domain do?
options: The domain of DNA polymerase that carries out synthesis.
The proofreading domain of DNA polymerase that excises mismatched nucleotides.
The enzyme that cuts the DNA ahead of the replication fork, lets it rotate and rejoins it, relieving torsional strain.
The enzyme that unwinds the two DNA strands so that they can be replicated.
questions.why: The slides draw the polymerase as a machine with two domains, POL and EXO: POL joins dNTPs into the new strand, EXO does the proofreading. When the polymerase puts in the wrong base it cuts that base out in the 3′→5′ direction and replaces it with the correct one; with proofreading in place the replication error rate can be as low as one error per billion nucleotides, and proofreading-defective mutants become ultramutators precisely because this domain has failed. The other three options describe the synthesis domain, the enzyme that relieves torsional strain and the enzyme that unwinds the duplex.

questions.q: What is the role of Exonuclease in DNA replication?
options: The enzyme that seals the final gap in a newly synthesised DNA strand.
The free-nucleotide raw material used when synthesising DNA.
The proofreading activity of DNA polymerase, which cuts out wrongly inserted bases.
The enzyme that synthesises DNA using RNA as a template.
questions.why: While it adds nucleotides, DNA polymerase uses its 3′→5′ exonuclease activity to look back over what it has just made: if the newly inserted base cannot pair with the template (A against G, for example), it cuts the mismatched base out and puts the correct one in. It is a read-then-fix mechanism whose direction is the opposite of the 5′→3′ of synthesis, which makes it very easy to muddle up. Exonuclease has a second job: removing the spent RNA primers on the lagging strand so that ligase can join the fragments; but this proofreading ability has a clinical cost, because it will also excise nucleoside analogue drugs from the DNA. The other three options describe the enzyme that seals the gap, the free-nucleotide raw material and the enzyme that uses RNA as a template.

questions.q: When the telomere becomes critically short and the cell stops dividing, what is the English name for this upper limit on “how many times a human cell can divide before it is forced to stop”?
questions.why: After each division the telomere shortens by about 50 to 200 base pairs because of the end-replication problem; once it reaches a critical length the cell stops dividing and enters senescence, and this limit is the Hayflick limit, the cell's division timer. Embryonic stem cells, some adult stem cells and germ cells maintain their telomeres with telomerase; cancer cells instead reactivate telomerase (about 90% of cancers upregulate it), so they can proliferate almost without limit. The other three options describe telomerase, the state of cellular senescence and the protein that trims over-long telomeres.

questions.q: During DNA replication, “_____” uses the energy of ATP to break the hydrogen bonds between the two DNA strands, separating the double helix into two template strands for the polymerase to copy.
questions.why: The mechanical action of helicase is to walk along the DNA and prise the helix open step by step, and at the same time single-strand binding protein is needed to stabilise the two separated strands so that they do not re-anneal. Another enzyme has to work at the same time: topoisomerase, because unwinding the helix generates torsional strain, and topoisomerase cuts and rejoins the DNA ahead of the replication fork to remove that strain. The set of basic pairings from lecture four is unwind (helicase), relieve strain (topoisomerase), primer (primase), extend and proofread (polymerase), remove primer (exonuclease) and seal (ligase). The other three options are respectively the enzyme that lays down primers, the enzyme that relieves strain and the enzyme that seals the gap, none of which separates the two strands.

questions.q: In this course, what does Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) refer to?
options: A primary cancer of the liver.
The state in which cells stop dividing without dying.
questions.why: HCC is a cancer arising from hepatocytes, and the lecturer uses the whole HCC story to show how basic biology turns into clinical application. The first case is vimentin (2D-PAGE separation → LC-MS/MS identification → verification by Western blot and qPCR → ELISA as a serum test); the second is circulating miRNA (miR-15b + miR-130b with AUC 0.981, sensitivity 98.25%, specificity 91.53%, accuracy 94.83%); the third is HBV integration and telomere length as prognostic markers. The other three options describe hepatocytes as a cell type, the wild-type baseline and the state of cellular senescence.

questions.q: What is a Hepatocyte?
options: A primary cancer of the liver.
The protein that shortens over-long telomeres by cutting away the t-loop.
The counting mechanism that turns cell division into a limit on “how many times one cell can divide”.
questions.why: The hepatocyte is the main functional cell of the liver, responsible for metabolism, albumin synthesis, detoxification and the production of bile; it plays three roles in this course. First, it is the protagonist of the Warburg effect: in the final step, glucose-6-phosphatase, which is specific to liver and kidney, returns free glucose to the blood, and a deficiency of this enzyme causes an energy crisis. Second, it is a cell that can be infected by HBV; once HBV DNA integrates into nearby genes it drives hepatocytes towards cancer. Third, it is where telomere is consumed: chronic damage causes hepatocyte turnover, the telomeres wear down, and later MYC reactivates telomerase, at which point HCC appears. The other three options describe liver cancer, the protein that trims over-long telomeres and the counting mechanism for the number of divisions.

questions.q: Because the polymerase can only add nucleotides to a 3′ end, the strand that has to be built piece by piece from short fragments is called what in English?
questions.why: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to a 3′ end, so synthesis is always 5′→3′; but the two template strands are antiparallel, so one of them is forced to be made segment by segment, each segment needing an RNA primer laid down by primase before the polymerase can take over, and the seams between fragments are finally sealed by ligase. The lagging strand is therefore slower and more troublesome. The other three options are respectively the leading strand, which can be copied smoothly in one go, the Y-shaped replication fork where the double helix is unwound, and the template strand that is read.

questions.q: In DNA replication, the strand whose new 3′ end keeps extending towards the replication fork, so that the polymerase can sit down once and write all the way along, is called “_____”.
questions.why: Because the polymerase only adds nucleotides to a 3′ end, continuous synthesis is in fact a consequence of the direction of the template strand rather than a special skill of the enzyme; it needs only a single RNA primer. The replication fork must still open up the duplex ahead of it at the same time: helicase unwinds it and topoisomerase relieves the torsional strain that builds up ahead. The other three options are respectively the replication bubble opened at each origin, the single-strand break that cuts only one strand, and the template strand that is read.

questions.q: In DNA replication, what does misincorporation mean?
options: The enzyme that seals the final gap in a newly synthesised DNA strand.
The polymerase placing a wrong base on the new strand.
The protein that shortens over-long telomeres by cutting away the t-loop.
The number of times human cells can divide before they are forced to stop.
questions.why: This is the first step of a replication error and also the point at which nucleoside analogue drugs make their move: the drug is taken up as if it were a nucleotide and the polymerase appends it to the end of the new strand. There are then two ways forward. If the exonuclease activity of p53 cuts the analogue out, the cell develops drug resistance; if subsequent DNA synthesis is blocked, the signal is converted into cell death signalling. The same analogue in the same cell can give different results, which shows that the effect of a drug depends not only on the drug itself but on the state of the cell at the time. The other three options describe the enzyme that seals the gap, the protein that trims over-long telomeres and the upper limit on the number of cell divisions.

questions.q: In this course, what does the name mitotic clock describe?
options: The protein that shortens over-long telomeres by cutting away the t-loop.
A single-strand break in which only one strand is cut while the other remains intact.
The counting mechanism that turns cell division into a limit on “how many times one cell can divide”.
The free-nucleotide raw material used when synthesising DNA.
questions.why: The ends of chromosomes carry telomeres, made of TTAGGG telomeric repeat sequences of 3 to 20 kb; because the polymerase cannot replicate the very end from scratch, the telomere shortens by about 50 to 200 bp at each division, and once it reaches the critical threshold (the Hayflick limit) the cell stops dividing and enters senescence. Stem cells and germ cells use telomerase to put the length back, and about 90% of cancers reactivate telomerase. In hepatocellular carcinoma, chronic damage drives compensatory hepatocyte proliferation and telomere exhaustion, and later upregulation of MYC restarts the telomere-extension mechanism; the telomeres lengthening again then becomes a prognostic marker. The other three options describe the protein that trims over-long telomeres, the single-strand break and the free-nucleotide raw material.

questions.q: In mismatch repair, what is the gene name of the MutLα complex that takes over the excision of the mismatched stretch so that the polymerase can put the correct bases back?
questions.why: MSH2 and MSH6 form MutSα (the mismatch recognition complex), which recognises the mismatch first; MLH1 and PMS2 form MutLα (the mismatch excision complex), which then takes over: when the polymerase has misincorporated on the lagging strand or slipped out a small loop, these two sets of proteins cut out the faulty stretch and re-synthesise it. MutLα does not itself know where the error is; it is called in by MutSα to do the processing. MLH1 expression can also be suppressed by promoter methylation, which is the real cause in many MSI tumours. The other three options are respectively the complex that recognises the mismatch and the polymerase genes that replicate the lagging and the leading strand.

questions.q: What role do MSH2/MSH6 play in DNA replication and repair?
options: The enzyme that seals the final gap in a newly synthesised DNA strand.
The enzyme that builds a new DNA chain, adding nucleotides only in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
The chemical bond that links adjacent nucleotides and forms the backbone of the DNA strand.
The first line of defence in mismatch repair, which specifically recognises replication mismatches.
questions.why: MSH2 and MSH6 form MutSα (the mismatch recognition complex), responsible for identifying bases on the new strand that cannot pair with the template; once they have been recognised the job is handed to MutLα (MLH1 and PMS2), the exonuclease cuts out the faulty stretch and the polymerase puts the correct bases back. The other variant, MSH2/MSH3 (MutSβ), is responsible for loop mismatches at repeat sequences; precisely because the two have to be distinguished, failure of MMR brings both an accumulation of mismatches and a change in microsatellite length. The other three options describe the enzyme that seals the gap, the enzyme that synthesises the new strand and the chemical bond that forms the DNA backbone.

questions.q: In lagging-strand replication, after the RNA primer has been removed and the polymerase has filled in, an unsealed cut still remains in the backbone; this “_____”, in which only one strand is cut while the other remains intact, is what DNA ligase has to seal.
questions.why: The job of DNA ligase is to join the 5′ phosphate to the 3′ hydroxyl, forming a phosphodiester bond that seals this nick; the lecturer's example is that if ligase is inhibited, cells still replicate, but the lagging strand is left with a pile of unsealed nicks and the cells can no longer divide properly. The other three options are respectively the replication bubble opened at each origin, the short stretches of DNA made first on the lagging strand and later joined together, and the free-nucleotide raw material used for synthesis.

questions.q: What is the English name for the short stretches of DNA made first on the lagging strand and later joined together by ligase (about 200 nucleotides each, beginning with a short RNA primer of about 10 nucleotides)?
questions.why: Each Okazaki fragment is about 200 nucleotides long and begins with a short RNA primer of about 10 nucleotides; the polymerase extends it from the 3′ end up to the next primer, and then the RNA primer is removed and the remaining gap is sealed by ligase. Because this has to be repeated thousands of times, replication of the lagging strand is actually slower than that of the leading strand, and every segment carries an extra round of laying down a primer, removing a primer and sealing the seam. Eukaryotic cells are more extreme still, with thousands of origins of replication active at once on a single chromosome, each running bidirectional replication forks. The other three options are respectively the Y-shaped opening where the double helix is unwound, the single-strand break and the enzyme that relieves torsional strain.

questions.q: On a eukaryotic chromosome, what is the English name for each position where a replication bubble opens and two replication forks run in opposite directions?
questions.why: Eukaryotic chromosomes are so large that they cannot be copied from one end, so thousands of origins are scattered across the DNA; each origin opens a replication bubble, and each bubble has two replication forks running in opposite directions; neighbouring forks meet in the end and replication is complete. Because the forks stop when they meet, replication does not need to know how long the whole chromosome is. The other three options are respectively the replication bubble where the DNA is pulled open, the Y-shaped replication fork where the double helix is unwound, and the single-strand break that cuts only one strand.

questions.q: What is a Phosphodiester bond?
options: The enzyme that synthesises DNA using RNA as a template.
The protein that shortens over-long telomeres by cutting away the t-loop.
The number of times human cells can divide before they are forced to stop.
The chemical bond that links adjacent nucleotides and forms the backbone of the DNA strand.
questions.why: The 3′ hydroxyl of one nucleotide and the 5′ phosphate of the next undergo condensation to form a 3′→5′ phosphodiester bond; when DNA ligase repairs the seam between Okazaki fragments it is catalysing the formation of exactly this bond, joining the 5′ phosphate to the 3′ hydroxyl. Once this bond has formed it cannot be undone, so DNA replication and repair can only ever move forwards, and the directionality of joining arises from it. The other three options describe the enzyme that uses RNA as a template, the protein that trims over-long telomeres and the upper limit on the number of cell divisions.

questions.q: In the lecturer's picture of DNA polymerase as a machine with two domains, what is the name of the domain that joins dNTPs into the new chain?
questions.why: POL is the structural domain of the polymerase, and what it does is join dNTPs into the new chain; the same molecule also has an EXO domain that does the proofreading. He draws the polymerase as a right hand: the fingers grip the template, the palm holds the new strand and the thumb pushes the nucleotide into place. The slides put the POL and EXO domains side by side to make the point that synthesis and proofreading are two functions on the same machine. The other three options are respectively the proofreading domain that excises mismatches, the RNA template component of telomerase and the transmission electron microscope.

questions.q: What does Pold1 refer to in DNA replication?
options: The gene for DNA polymerase epsilon, which replicates the leading strand.
A double-mutant mouse that has lost the proofreading ability of both polymerases.
The gene for DNA polymerase delta, which replicates the lagging strand.
The domain of DNA polymerase that carries out synthesis.
questions.why: Pol δ works on the lagging strand at the replication fork and takes over the extension of every Okazaki fragment, while Pol ε is responsible for the leading strand. Pol δ carries 3′→5′ proofreading exonuclease activity, and once this activity is broken by a mutation (proofreading-defective) the replication error rate soars and the cell becomes an ultramutator. Pold1 and Pole represent the gatekeepers of the two strands respectively; he sets these two mutations alongside the Mlh1 knockout in order to show that replication proofreading and MMR are different lines of defence. The other three options describe the polymerase gene for the leading strand, the double-mutant mouse that loses proofreading on both strands at once and the synthesis domain of the polymerase.

questions.q: In DNA replication, what is the “_____” polymerase gene that extends the new strand on the leading strand and carries 3′→5′ proofreading exonuclease activity?
questions.why: Pol ε carries proofreading exonuclease activity just as Pol δ does; the lecturer used proofreading-defective Pole mutants to generate ultramutator tumours and compared them with the Pold1 mutation, the Mlh1 knockout and the Pole e/e Pold1 e/e double mutant, showing that each of the two strands of replication has its own gatekeeper. Pol ε handles the leading strand and Pol δ the lagging strand, each guarding its own end, and his comparison experiment is precisely what demonstrates that the two lines of defence can fail independently of one another. The other three options are respectively the polymerase gene for the lagging strand, the synthesis domain of the polymerase and the proofreading activity that excises mismatches.

questions.q: In the lecturer's experiment comparing the two lines of defence, replication proofreading and MMR, which group of mice best demonstrates that both are indispensable and that losing both is worse?
options: A single-strand break in which only one strand is cut while the other remains intact.
The proofreading domain of DNA polymerase that excises mismatched nucleotides.
A double-mutant mouse that has lost the proofreading ability of both polymerases.
questions.why: e/e denotes the exonuclease-deficient allele; this double mutant switches off the proofreading ability of both Pol ε and Pol δ at once, so both lines of defence fall at the same time, which is why this group of mice has the shortest survival and the most tumours in his tumour incidence table, and it is used to show that proofreading and MMR are two independently effective lines of defence, that neither can be dispensed with and that losing both is worse. The other three options describe the normal baseline, the single-strand break and the proofreading domain of the polymerase.

questions.q: What is the function of Primase in DNA replication?
options: The enzyme that builds a new DNA chain, adding nucleotides only in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
The enzyme that lays down the short RNA primer so that DNA polymerase has a starting point.
The enzyme that unwinds the two DNA strands so that they can be replicated.
The enzyme that cuts the DNA ahead of the replication fork, lets it rotate and rejoins it, relieving torsional strain.
questions.why: DNA polymerase cannot start from nothing: it needs a free 3′ hydroxyl before it can add the first nucleotide. Primase makes an RNA primer of about 10 nucleotides to provide this starting point, the polymerase takes over from there and extends 5′→3′, and the RNA primer is later removed with the gap sealed by ligase. Every segment of the lagging strand needs a fresh primer, and in eukaryotic cells each origin of replication also has to be primed first, so replication must begin at an origin and its direction is set there. The other three options describe the enzyme that synthesises the new strand, the enzyme that unwinds the duplex and the enzyme that relieves torsional strain.

questions.q: What is the English name for the correction mechanism in which DNA polymerase checks back over what it has just made while synthesising, cutting out and replacing a wrongly placed base?
questions.why: Base pairing alone gives an error rate of about one in a hundred thousand bases; the 3′→5′ exonuclease activity sits on the polymerase like a proofreader, checking each newly added base against the template strand and cutting out and replacing anything that does not pair, and only with MMR added does the overall error rate fall to about one in a billion bases. The same mechanism can also cut away nucleoside analogue drugs, which is a source of drug resistance; a polymerase that has lost proofreading generates a flood of mutations, giving the tumour many neoantigens, and it responds better rather than worse to immune checkpoint inhibitors. The other three options describe the single-strand break, the misplacement of a base itself, and the tumour no longer responding to a drug.

questions.q: In DNA replication, what does a Replication bubble refer to?
options: The bubble where the DNA is pulled open, with one replication fork running on each side.
The enzyme that unwinds the two DNA strands so that they can be replicated.
The number of times human cells can divide before they are forced to stop.
questions.why: Replication does not run from one end of the chromosome to the other; eukaryotic chromosomes are so long that thousands of origins are opened at the same time, and each origin is a replication bubble with a replication fork running from each end in opposite directions. The net effect is that thousands of replication forks are running on the same chromosome at once, which keeps the replication time within an acceptable range. The multiple bubbles seen in electron micrographs are direct evidence of this. The clinical relevance is direct too: most anticancer drugs that damage DNA target the cells that are being replicated thousands of times. The other three options describe the unwinding enzyme, the upper limit on the number of cell divisions and the wild-type baseline.

questions.q: In DNA replication, the Y-shaped opening where the double helix is unwound and copied as it opens is called “_____”.
questions.why: The replication fork has two arms, which are the two template strands; as it advances, helicase opens the double helix, topoisomerase relieves the twisting ahead, primase lays down the RNA primer and DNA polymerase lengthens the new strand piece by piece. On one side is the continuous leading strand, on the other the lagging strand assembled from fragments; each origin opens a bubble, and each bubble has two forks running in opposite directions. The other three options are respectively the replication bubble opened at each origin, the short stretches of DNA made first on the lagging strand and then joined, and the single-strand break that cuts only one strand.

questions.q: On a eukaryotic chromosome, what is the English name for each stretch of DNA that has its own origin, its own pair of oppositely directed forks, and can be replicated independently?
questions.why: Replication on a eukaryotic chromosome is not completed in one go but is divided into many replicons, each with its own origin and two forks running in opposite directions; when neighbouring forks meet, replication is finished there, simply because they have run into new DNA that someone else has already made. The benefit of this design is that replication can proceed in parallel, which is how a human chromosome can be replicated in a relatively short time instead of being copied from one end to the other. The other three options are respectively the replication bubble opened at each origin, the single-strand break and the enzyme that relieves torsional strain.

questions.q: What does Reverse transcriptase refer to?
options: The enzyme that builds a new DNA chain, adding nucleotides only in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
The proofreading activity of DNA polymerase, which cuts out wrongly inserted bases.
The enzyme that synthesises DNA using RNA as a template.
The exonuclease that removes the RNA primer from the DNA.
questions.why: Ordinary DNA replication is DNA → DNA; reverse transcriptase turns it round to make RNA → DNA. It requires an RNA template, which is why versions with a built-in template are especially useful: telomerase is a reverse transcriptase with a built-in RNA template and uses it to extend the 3′ overhang at the end of the chromosome. HBV also replicates by reverse transcription, while retroviruses reverse-transcribe the whole genome into DNA and then integrate it into the host. The other three options describe the enzyme that synthesises a new strand using DNA as a template, the exonuclease responsible for proofreading and the exonuclease that removes RNA primers.

questions.q: In the lagging-strand replication workflow, the RNA primer has to be removed and replaced with DNA; which enzyme recognises the RNA–DNA junction and cuts away the RNA portion?
options: The exonuclease that removes the RNA primer from the DNA.
The enzyme that seals the final gap in a newly synthesised DNA strand.
The enzyme that cuts the DNA ahead of the replication fork, lets it rotate and rejoins it, relieving torsional strain.
The enzyme that builds a new DNA chain, adding nucleotides only in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
questions.why: Each Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand begins with an RNA primer, and once the polymerase has lengthened the fragment the RNA primer in front becomes a redundant foreign object that must be replaced with DNA; RNase H recognises the RNA–DNA junction and cuts away the RNA portion, the gap that is left is filled in by DNA polymerase and ligase does the final sealing. The RNA primer has to be replaced with DNA, otherwise the new strand is left with a seam of RNA mixed with DNA, which is bad for subsequent replication and also affects stability. The other three options describe the enzyme that seals the gap, the enzyme that relieves torsional strain and the enzyme that synthesises the new strand.

questions.q: What does Semi-conservative replication mean?
options: The third of the three models of DNA replication: the old strands are broken up and mixed into the new strands.
The enzyme that seals the final gap in a newly synthesised DNA strand.
The protein that shortens over-long telomeres by cutting away the t-loop.
Every new DNA duplex consists of one old strand plus one new strand.
questions.why: This is the rule of DNA replication and also the conclusion of the Meselson–Stahl isotope-labelling experiment: the DNA separates into single strands, each serves as a template for a new strand, and so every daughter molecule contains exactly one parental strand and one newly synthesised strand. There is only one point of discrimination: after the first round the hybrid molecules appear; conservative replication would give an untouched parental molecule alongside a completely new one, whereas dispersive mixes old and new fragments into both strands, and the experimental results support the semi-conservative model. The other three options describe the dispersive model, the enzyme that seals the gap and the protein that trims over-long telomeres.

questions.q: When the telomere shrinks to a critical length and the cell stops dividing without being cleared away but stays in the tissue no longer proliferating, that state is called “_____”.
questions.why: When the telomere shrinks to a critical length the cell stops dividing and enters senescence, and that is the Hayflick limit; it differs from apoptosis in that the cell is not cleared away and stays in the tissue but no longer proliferates. The difference matters in cancer: a cell that has already senesced may still bypass this brake if the growth signal goes out of control; the most direct example is p53, since about 40% of cancers carry p53 mutations, which amounts to removing the brake. The other three options describe the upper limit on the number of cell divisions, the telomerase that puts the telomere back and the antisense oligonucleotide that degrades TERT mRNA.

questions.q: What is the role of Telomerase in telomere maintenance?
options: The protein that shortens over-long telomeres by cutting away the t-loop.
DNA polymerase cannot replicate the very end of a linear chromosome, so the telomere shortens at every division.
The special enzyme that can rebuild chromosome ends, which most cancer cells switch back on.
The RNA template component of telomerase.
questions.why: Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase with a built-in RNA template: it uses the RNA it carries (complementary to the 3′ overhang) as a template and adds GGTTAG repeat sequences piece by piece, then moves itself along and adds the next stretch, so that the last incomplete gap on the lagging strand is filled in. Telomerase is almost switched off in normal somatic cells, so the telomere gets a little shorter with each division; ESCs, some adult stem cells and germ cells keep it active, whereas cancer cells switch it back on to divide without limit, with about 90% of cancers upregulating telomerase. The other three options describe the protein that trims over-long telomeres, the end-replication problem itself and the RNA template component of telomerase.

questions.q: On the slides of lecture four in this course, what instrument does TEM refer to?
options: The enzyme that seals the final gap in a newly synthesised DNA strand.
The enzyme that cuts the DNA ahead of the replication fork, lets it rotate and rejoins it, relieving torsional strain.
questions.why: TEM uses a beam of electrons to pass through an ultrathin specimen; because different structures scatter electrons to different degrees it forms a high-resolution image, in principle one in which a single protein can be seen. The lecturer's slide is a TEM photograph of a mouse L cell at 15,000× magnification, with the labelled organelles corresponding one-to-one with the cartoon cell beside it; he says explicitly that the chromatin images from electron microscopy do not have to be memorised. The other three options describe the enzyme that seals the gap, the enzyme that relieves torsional strain and hepatocytes.

questions.q: The DNA strand that is read during replication, whose sequence determines the sequence of the new strand (the antisense strand), is called “_____”.
questions.why: Both strands are read, but at any one moment only one is the template of the moment. The template strand is the antisense strand, and its sequence determines the sequence of the new strand; the corresponding sense strand has the same sequence as the newly made RNA except that T is replaced by U, because RNA polymerase reads the template strand directly to make RNA instead of first making DNA and then transcribing it. The key constraint is direction: RNA polymerase can only extend 5′→3′, so it can only travel along the template strand in the 3′→5′ direction; the same rule of direction also determines the division of labour between the leading and lagging strands. The other three options are respectively the leading strand, which can be copied smoothly in one go, the lagging strand, which is assembled from fragments, and the short stretches of DNA made first on the lagging strand and then joined.

questions.q: What is the name of the template RNA that telomerase carries with it, the human telomerase RNA component, and uses to add TTAGGG telomeric repeat sequences?
questions.why: Telomerase itself is a reverse transcriptase: it makes DNA using RNA, so it has to carry its own template. TERC is that template RNA; it pairs with the 3′ overhang at the chromosome end so that the enzyme can add TTAGGG telomeric repeat sequences, while TERT is the catalytically active protein component. If both TERC and TERT are normal the telomere can be maintained; if telomerase fails, the cell loses a stretch with every round of replication and eventually runs into the Hayflick limit and senescence. The other three options describe telomerase as a whole, the antisense oligonucleotide that degrades TERT mRNA and the protein that trims over-long telomeres.

questions.q: What is the function of Topoisomerase in DNA replication?
options: The enzyme that unwinds the two DNA strands so that they can be replicated.
The enzyme that lays down the short RNA primer so that DNA polymerase has a starting point.
The enzyme that cuts the DNA ahead of the replication fork, lets it rotate and rejoins it, relieving torsional strain.
The enzyme that seals the final gap in a newly synthesised DNA strand.
questions.why: The DNA duplex is like a double helix, and pulling it open builds up over-winding tension ahead. Topoisomerase's solution is to cut the DNA backbone temporarily, let it rotate and relax, then rejoin it (one of the two strands is cut, and ligase seals it afterwards). It is central to the ADC treatment strategy: inhibiting topoisomerase I leaves the tangle ahead of the replication fork unable to unwind, which accumulates into double-strand breaks and kills the cell. The other three options describe the enzyme that unwinds, the one that lays down primers and the one that seals the gap.

questions.q: After telomeres have been lengthened, the ends of the chromosome grow a t-loop that is hard to handle; the protein that cuts away the surplus t-loop like a pair of scissors and brings the telomere length back into a manageable range is “_____”.
questions.why: TZAP acts like a pair of scissors to cut away the surplus t-loop and bring the telomere length back into a manageable range; over-long telomeres have clinical significance in their own right: in liver cancer the patients with the longest telomeres, the top 10%, actually have worse recurrence-free survival. The other three options describe the telomerase that lengthens telomeres, the RNA template that telomerase carries and the enzyme that relieves torsional strain.

questions.q: In the logic of predictive biomarkers, what does wild type refer to?
options: A primary cancer of the liver.
The state in which cells stop dividing without dying.
The protein that shortens over-long telomeres by cutting away the t-loop.
questions.why: Wild type is the baseline used for comparison with the mutated version; K-Ras is the best example: wild-type K-Ras is activated only when the upstream EGFR signals, whereas the mutant version activates itself and keeps sending out growth signals whether or not there is an upstream signal. This contrast is the whole logic of a predictive biomarker: with mutant K-Ras the downstream pathway is already switched on, so the anti-EGFR drug cetuximab does not work; only wild-type K-Ras has any chance of responding. The figures the lecturer gives are that KRAS mutants survive less well (p = 0.016), and that KRAS G12C accounts for 13% of lung adenocarcinoma and 3% of colorectal cancer. The other three options describe liver cancer, the state of cellular senescence and the protein that trims over-long telomeres.
